title: US Web Dominance Waning, Report Says
text:
US Web Dominance Waning, Report Says

# US Web Dominance Waning, Report Says

4 September 2000 

 While the United States still holds the largest share of the world's Internet users, European and Asian nations will soon surpass the US as the Internet becomes more multilingual and more dependent on wireless networks, according to a report released Friday. 

The report, issued by the US Internet Council (USIC), an industry-funded public policy group, said the US accounts for 136 million - roughly 45 percent - of all Internet users, with Europe and Asia claiming 83 million and 68.9 million, respectively. 

By 2005, however, the number of Web surfers worldwide could exceed 1 billion, with 70 percent of those users located outside of North America, the report said. 

The USIC report notes that while just 50 percent of all Internet users are native English speakers, English language Web sites continue to dominate the Net: 78 percent of all Web sites are currently in English, while 96 percent of all e-commerce sites are in English. As European and Asian nations begin to dominate the Web over the next five years, English will lose its dominant position on the Web in favor of increased linguistic diversity. 

"The growth in the number of non-English speaking web sites, combined with a rapidly rising number of Internet users in Asia and Europe, is transforming the Internet from an American-dominated medium to a true international communications backbone," said Bill Myers, CEO of the council. 

"Although English-speaking users in North America continue to be the largest single block of the online population, already there appear to be at least 15 million more users in Asia and Europe combined." 

Perhaps the greatest edge that European and Asian nations hold, Myers said, lies in their development of wireless Web technologies. The report notes that both Europe and Japan are way ahead in this department, while the US is burdened with numerous competing standards that have resulted in interoperability problems and incompatible services. 

By way of example, more than 300 million people worldwide now use mobile phones. Among those, Europe is leading with the highest mobile penetration rates, with Asian nations following close behind. The US, on the other hand, currently lags behind 22 other nations with just 27.6 percent of its citizens mobile-phone equipped. 

The USIC argues that as wireless platforms begin to match PC quality within the next few years, companies in Asia and Europe will begin to adapt the e-commerce model to rely more on wireless networks, an outcome that could erode US leadership in e-commerce. 

A recent White Paper issued by International Data Corp. appears to hold up that assertion, noting that by 2003, the US will account for just 44 percent of the total global e-commerce market, down from 61.7 percent in 1999. On the other hand, Europe stands to increase its market share from 18.7 percent to 31.2 percent over the same period, with Japan's share rising from 10.3 to 15.3 percent. 

For a copy of the report, check out www.usic.org. 

Reported by Newsbytes, www.newsbytes.com.
